newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia tackles emotive issue of housing reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russia tackles emotive issue of housing reforms.

text.p: Russia's government meets on Monday to consider sweeping housing reform, one of the most emotive challenges facing President Boris Yeltsin's new team of young reformers.

Yeltsin will chair the session, intended to set guidelines for replacing blanket rent subsidies with a system where aid is to become more selective to help the most needy and subsidised household utility bills are to be phased out.

Low housing costs and energy bills are among the few comforts left over from Soviet times under tough reforms. Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov says removing them could provoke a public outcry and even put the government's future in doubt.
"We are not against housing and communal reform. We are against rates and reforms where payment for services is fully shouldered by the people," Luzhkov said last week.
Luzhkov is expected to put Moscow's case for exemption from the reform plan during Monday's session.

Luzhkov, who has criticised some government policies in what is widely seen as a long-term bid to become president, says Yeltsin has assured him Moscow can have a degree of independence in housing reforms because the capital is a special case.

Other city mayors and regional leaders are also expected to attend the meeting. They are supposed to draw up their own regional programmes of housing reform, based closely on the government's recommendations, by August 1.

Under government plans, housing and utilities are intended to become a loss-free sector by the year 2003. Those plans, saving the government a vast amount of money, will be outlined on Monday by young First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.
Critics say the changes will force ordinary Russians to pay much higher bills. The government says their plans will wipe out the monopolies of energy and water suppliers, reducing tariffs.

The changes, which Yeltsin hopes will please the International Monetary Fund, are central to the reform plans of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's government, which has been reshuffled over the last two months to promote young reformers.

The government has also vowed to restructure inefficient monopolies such as the gas and electricity industries, boost tax collection and cut the 1997 budget by one-fifth because of a shortfall of revenues.

But housing reforms will have a particularly direct impact on ordinary Russians and any popular resistance is likely to grow if the government fails to carry out promises to wipe out large wage and pension arrears.

"This important issue should be examined very thoroughly. Everything should be thought out well, and then an approach to reforming the housing and communal sphere should be worked out," Chernomyrdin told Itar-Tass news agency on Saturday.

Luzhkov's worries over housing reforms have highlighted the problems the government could face if regional leaders resist reforms. In many cases, implementation of centrally-planned reforms depends largely on the leaders in the regions.

In a sign of the government's awareness of the role of the regions, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais was due to attend a meeting of regional economic leaders in the Siberian city of Krasnoyarsk on Monday.
Chubais has said he wants to discuss drawing up the 1998 budget with these and other regional leaders.
Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev will also leave Moscow for the regions to attend a meeting of regional leaders in Khabarovsk in Russia's Far East on Tuesday.
